title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hook: a day has moods that arrive roughly on schedule. one classical text gives each stretch of time a dosha
carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, and Sushruta's word for well: svastha, ending in a clear, content mind. When you asked how the mind was, what came back? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

Early morning, the body is slow to get going, and the snooze button looks very reasonable. Around noon, hunger gets sharp and so does the temper. Late afternoon, attention starts to scatter like leaves in a parking lot. A day has moods, and they tend to arrive roughly on schedule. The Ashtanga Hridaya noticed a pattern like that too. It doesn't hand out a timetable to the minute. It gives each part of the day a dosha. Today: the doshas on the clock.

In paraphrase, the verse says this. The doshas run through the whole body, and they rise in turn: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end. The beginning, middle and end of what? Of a life, of a day, of a night, and of a meal. So the same three-part pattern is laid over four different clocks. Take the day. At its beginning, kapha, the heavy, slow, steady one. In the middle, pitta, the hot and sharp. Toward the end, vata, the light and moving. Lay it over a life and it reads the same way: kapha in childhood, pitta in the middle years, vata in old age. Lay it over a meal: heaviness right after eating, then the heat of digestion, then lightness. Notice what the text does not say. It doesn't give exact hours. Beginning, middle and end are all it offers, and how anyone divides those up is a later question. And notice the tone. In this verse the doshas are simply taking turns, the way the light changes across a day. That's the gift for noticing. A slow morning may not be a character flaw. A sharp noon may not be a personal failing. Some of it may be the hour. On this path, that's a way of looking, not a rule to live by, and never a diagnosis. Anything about sleep or energy that keeps on is a question for a doctor.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find where you are on the clock. Notice what part of the day it is right now: beginning, middle, or end. Then look for that part's quality in your body. Is there heaviness? Heat? Lightness, a skittering mind? Don't judge what you find. Just notice whether the hour and the body agree today, or don't. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here. The bell holds the time.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, on the clock: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end. Today's word.

fork.setup: it's late afternoon and your attention is scattering like leaves. on the text's clock, which dosha is having its turn?
fork.reveal: vata comes at the end: of the day, the night, the meal and a life. light and moving, like scattering leaves.

original.note: Sanskrit: time. Ayurveda reads the doshas against time: a day, a night, a meal, a life.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dosha is a fixed type you're stuck with.
what it means: the doshas take turns, rising at the beginning, middle and end of a day, a night, a meal and a life.
what a scholar hears: vayo'horatribhuktanam te 'ntamadhyadigah kramat, of age, day, night and meal, they hold the end, middle and beginning in turn (Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 1.8).
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 1.8 (the doshas pervade the body and rise at the end, middle and beginning of life, day, night and meal: vata, pitta and kapha in turn)
